questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Find the value of (6⁴ × 36²) ÷ 216².

solution.concept: Write every term as a power of the same base: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ and aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ
solution.explanation: 36² = (6²)² = 6⁴ and 216² = (6³)² = 6⁶. So the expression is 6⁴ × 6⁴ ÷ 6⁶ = 6⁴⁺⁴⁻⁶ = 6² = 36.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6, 216 and 1,296 (6¹, 6³ and 6⁴) come from writing 36² as 6³, 6⁵ or 6⁶ by mistake, or from multiplying instead of adding the powers.

solution.concept: Add the two fractions over the common denominator (√11 − √7)(√11 + √7) = 11 − 7
solution.explanation: The common denominator is (√11)² − (√7)² = 4. The numerator is (√11 + √7)² + (√11 − √7)² = 2(11 + 7) = 36. So the value is 36 ÷ 4 = 9.
solution.why_others_wrong: 18 divides by 2 instead of 4; 4.5 divides by 8; 36 forgets the denominator.

solution.concept: The cube root of a decimal has one-third as many decimal places; write a mixed number as an improper fraction before taking its root
solution.why_others_wrong: 11.25 takes ∛0.000729 as 0.9; 2.75 takes √(1 9/16) as 1 + ¾; 1.25 drops the quotient 1.

solution.concept: √(a + b ± 2√ab) = √a ± √b (with √a > √b): find two numbers whose sum is 10 and product is 21
solution.explanation: 7 + 3 = 10 and 7 × 3 = 21, so 10 + 2√21 = (√7 + √3)² and 10 − 2√21 = (√7 − √3)². Since √7 > √3, the roots are √7 + √3 and √7 − √3, and their difference is 2√3.
steps: Need a + b = 10 and ab = 21 ⇒ a = 7, b = 3
solution.why_others_wrong: 2√7 is the sum of the two roots, not the difference; 2√10 treats √(10 ± 2√21) as √10 ± something that cancels the wrong way; 0 assumes the two roots are equal.

solution.concept: Telescoping: 1/(n(n + 2)) = ½ × (1/n − 1/(n + 2))
solution.explanation: Each term splits as ½(1/n − 1/(n + 2)). Adding from n = 1 to n = 19 (odd n only), the middle terms cancel and the sum is ½(1 − 1/21) = ½ × 20/21 = 10/21.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20/21 forgets the factor ½; 11/21 adds 1/21 instead of subtracting it; 10/19 stops the series at 1/19.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
1, 8, 9, 64, 25, 216, ?

solution.concept: Alternate positions follow different rules: odd positions are squares, even positions are cubes

solution.why_others_wrong: 343 = 7³ ignores the alternation; 36 = 6² and 125 = 5³ use the wrong base.

Find the missing number (?) in the series:
120, ?, 168, 195, 224, 255

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
1, 3, 8, 21, 55, ?

solution.explanation: 8 = 3 × 3 − 1, 21 = 3 × 8 − 3, 55 = 3 × 21 − 8, so the next term is 3 × 55 − 21 = 144. (These are alternate Fibonacci numbers.)

solution.why_others_wrong: 89 is the next difference, not the next term; 134 and 155 use × 3 − 31 or × 3 − 10.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve the pair of equations given below. Which relation between x and y is true for every pair of roots?
I. x² − 21x + 110 = 0
II. y² − 15y + 54 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise by splitting the middle term; compare the smallest x with the largest y
solution.explanation: x = 10 or 11 and y = 6 or 9. The smallest x (10) is greater than the largest y (9), so x > y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y and x ≤ y come from reading the root signs as negative.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find all the roots of equations I and II, then compare x with y.
I. x² + 11x + 30 = 0
II. y² + 7y + 12 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: With all coefficients positive, both roots are negative
solution.explanation: x = −5 or −6 and y = −3 or −4. The largest x (−5) is smaller than the smallest y (−4), so x < y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y comes from dropping the minus signs (5, 6 against 3, 4).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equations I and II below are quadratics in x and y. After solving them, mark the relation that always holds.
I. 2x² − 9x + 10 = 0
II. 3y² − 11y + 10 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: A shared root makes the relation non-strict
solution.explanation: x = 2 or 2.5 and y = 2 or 1.67. Every x is at least as large as every y, and x = y = 2 is possible, so x ≥ y.
steps: x = 2, y = 2 gives x = y; all other pairs x > y
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y misses the common root 2.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
One equation below is quadratic and the other linear. Solve both and choose the correct relation between x and y.
I. 2x² + 5x − 12 = 0
II. 5y − 2 = 2y − 6.5

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Solve the linear equation directly; a quadratic root on each side of y means no relation holds
solution.explanation: I: x = 1.5 or −4. II: 3y = −4.5, so y = −1.5. x = 1.5 is greater than y but x = −4 is smaller, so the relation cannot be established.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y uses only the positive root 1.5; x ≤ y uses only −4.
solution.final_answer: Option A: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The equations below have irrational coefficients. Solve them and choose the relation between x and y, if any, that holds for all roots.
I. x² − 7√2x + 24 = 0
II. y² − 6√3y + 24 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Quadratics with surd coefficients: find two roots from their sum and product
solution.explanation: For I, the roots have sum 7√2 and product 24: 3√2 and 4√2 (≈ 4.24 and 5.66). For II, the roots have sum 6√3 and product 24: 2√3 and 4√3 (≈ 3.46 and 6.93). x = 4.24 is above y = 3.46 but below y = 6.93, so no relation holds.
steps: All roots are positive, so compare squares: x² ∈ {18, 32}, y² ∈ {12, 48}
solution.shortcut: Compare the squares of the positive roots: 18, 32 against 12, 48.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y compares only 32 with 48; x ≥ y compares only 18 with 12.
solution.final_answer: Option C: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Both equations below have fractional roots. Determine the roots and select the correct relationship between x and y.
I. 6x² − 7x + 2 = 0
II. 12y² − 7y + 1 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise with a ≠ 1 and compare fractional roots
solution.explanation: x = 1/2 or 2/3 and y = 1/3 or 1/4. The smallest x (0.5) is greater than the largest y (0.33), so x > y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y comes from taking the reciprocals (2, 1.5 against 3, 4) instead of the roots.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The HCF of two numbers is 14 and their LCM is 420. If one of the numbers is 70, what is the other number?

solution.concept: For two numbers, product of the numbers = HCF × LCM
solution.explanation: 70 × other = 14 × 420 = 5,880, so the other number is 5,880 ÷ 70 = 84. Check: HCF(70, 84) = 14 and LCM(70, 84) = 420.
solution.why_others_wrong: 98, 56 and 42 are multiples of 14, but with 70 their LCM is 490, 280 and 210, not 420.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the unit digit of 1! + 2! + 3! + … + 50!?

solution.concept: From 5! onwards every factorial contains 2 × 5, so it ends in 0
solution.explanation: 5!, 6!, …, 50! all end in 0. So only 1! + 2! + 3! + 4! = 1 + 2 + 6 + 24 = 33 decides the unit digit, which is 3.
steps: 5! = 120 and every later factorial is a multiple of 10
solution.why_others_wrong: 0 assumes every term ends in 0; 4 and 9 are the unit digits of 4! and of 1 + 2 + 6 only.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The five-digit number 2a43b, where a and b are digits, is divisible by 72. What is the value of a × b?

solution.concept: 72 = 8 × 9 with 8 and 9 co-prime: test divisibility by 8 (last three digits) and by 9 (digit sum)
solution.explanation: For 8, the last three digits 43b must be a multiple of 8; 432 is the only one, so b = 2. For 9, the digit sum 2 + a + 4 + 3 + 2 = 11 + a must be a multiple of 9, so a = 7. The number is 27,432 = 72 × 381, and a × b = 14.
solution.why_others_wrong: 16, 18 and 12 come from pairs (a, b) that pass only one of the two tests, for example a = 9, b = 2 or b = 6.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the smallest number which, when divided by 8, 12 and 15, leaves remainders 5, 9 and 12 respectively?

solution.concept: If divisor − remainder is the same for every divisor (here 3), the number = k × LCM − that common difference
solution.explanation: 8 − 5 = 12 − 9 = 15 − 12 = 3, so the number is 3 short of a common multiple of 8, 12 and 15. LCM(8, 12, 15) = 120, so the smallest such number is 120 − 3 = 117.
solution.why_others_wrong: 123 adds the 3 instead of subtracting; 237 is the next such number after 117, not the smallest; 113 subtracts 7.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The sum of two positive numbers is 216 and their HCF is 27. How many such pairs of numbers are possible?

solution.concept: Write the numbers as 27a and 27b with a and b co-prime
solution.explanation: 27a + 27b = 216 gives a + b = 8. Co-prime pairs with a < b are (1, 7) and (3, 5); (2, 6) and (4, 4) share a factor. So the pairs are (27, 189) and (81, 135): 2 pairs.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 and 4 include (2, 6) or (4, 4), whose HCF would be 54 or 108; 1 misses (3, 5).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A water tank is 35% full. After 84 litres of water are poured in, it is 56% full. What is the capacity of the tank?

solution.concept: The added water equals the change in the percentage filled
solution.explanation: The 84 litres raise the level from 35% to 56%, that is, by 21% of the capacity. So capacity = 84 ÷ 0.21 = 400 litres.
solution.why_others_wrong: 240 treats 84 litres as 35% of the tank; 150 treats it as 56%; 420 uses 20% instead of 21%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The price of a television was raised by 25%, then cut by 20% in a sale, and later raised by 10%. What is the overall change in its price?

solution.concept: Successive percentage changes multiply: final = original × (1 + r₁)(1 + r₂)(1 + r₃)
solution.explanation: Multiplying factors: 1.25 × 0.80 × 1.10 = 1.10. The price ends 10% above where it started.
solution.shortcut: A 25% rise followed by a 20% cut cancel exactly (5/4 × 4/5 = 1), leaving only the 10% rise.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15% adds the percentages (25 − 20 + 10); 5% ignores the last rise; 'No change' stops after the first two steps.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A car bought for ₹6,25,000 loses 20% of its value in the first year and 12% of its value at the start of each later year. What is its value after 3 years?

solution.concept: Depreciation on the reducing value: multiply by (1 − rate) year by year
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹3,50,000 subtracts 20% + 12% + 12% = 44% of the original price; ₹4,40,000 is the value after 2 years; ₹3,52,000 applies 20% again in year 3.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Amit's income is 25% more than Bina's. Amit spends 70% of his income and Bina spends 75% of hers. If Amit saves ₹1,500 more than Bina, what is Amit's income?

solution.concept: Express both savings in terms of one income
solution.explanation: Let Bina's income be B. Amit's income is 1.25B and he saves 30% of it, 0.375B. Bina saves 0.25B. The difference 0.125B = 1,500, so B = 12,000 and Amit's income = 15,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹12,000 is Bina's income; ₹18,750 is 1.25 × 15,000; ₹20,000 takes the 1,500 as 7.5% of Amit's income.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In a test, 72% of the candidates passed in Mathematics, 65% passed in English and 18% failed in both. If 495 candidates passed in both subjects, how many candidates took the test?

solution.concept: Sets: passed in at least one = 100% − failed in both; both = M + E − at least one
solution.explanation: 82% passed in at least one subject. So both = 72% + 65% − 82% = 55%. 55% of the total is 495, so the total is 495 ÷ 0.55 = 900.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,100 takes 495 as 45% of the candidates; 825 takes it as 60%; 990 takes it as 50%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A town's population of 50,000 grows by 10% every year. At the end of each year, after the growth, 1,000 people move out. What is the population at the end of 2 years?

solution.concept: Apply growth and the fixed outflow year by year; the outflow of year 1 also misses the growth of year 2
solution.why_others_wrong: 58,500 grows 50,000 for both years and subtracts 2,000 at the end, ignoring that the first 1,000 would not have grown; 60,500 ignores migration; 59,500 subtracts only once.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The incomes of A and B are in the ratio 4 : 3 and their expenditures are in the ratio 3 : 2. If each saves ₹6,000 a month, what is A's monthly income?

solution.concept: Income − expenditure = saving; set up the expenditure ratio
solution.explanation: Let the incomes be 4x and 3x. Expenditures are 4x − 6,000 and 3x − 6,000, in the ratio 3 : 2. So 2(4x − 6,000) = 3(3x − 6,000), which gives x = 6,000. A's income = 4x = ₹24,000.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If (3a + 5b) : (3a − 5b) = 7 : 3, what is a : b?

solution.concept: Cross-multiply a proportion: p : q = r : s means ps = qr
solution.shortcut: Componendo-dividendo: 3a : 5b = (7 + 3) : (7 − 3) = 5 : 2, so a : b = 25 : 6.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 : 25 is inverted; 5 : 3 and 10 : 3 stop at 3a : 5b = 5 : 2 without dividing by 3 and 5 correctly.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: ₹10,800 is divided among A, B and C so that A gets two-thirds of what B and C together get, and B gets one-fourth of what A and C together get. What is B's share?

solution.concept: If X gets p/q of what the others get, X's share = p/(p + q) of the total
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹4,320 is A's (and C's) share; ₹2,700 takes B as one-fourth of the total; ₹1,800 takes it as one-sixth.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Three numbers are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 5 and the sum of their squares is 1,368. What is the largest number?

solution.concept: Write the numbers as 2k, 3k and 5k
solution.explanation: (2k)² + (3k)² + (5k)² = 38k² = 1,368, so k² = 36 and k = 6 (the numbers are positive). The numbers are 12, 18 and 30, and the largest is 30.
solution.why_others_wrong: 18 is the middle number; 36 is k², not 5k; 24 corresponds to k = 4.8, whose squares add up to only 875.52.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Ravi is 6 years older than Sunil. Five years ago, Ravi's age was 1.5 times Sunil's age. What is Ravi's present age?

solution.concept: Write both ages five years ago in terms of one unknown
solution.explanation: Let Sunil be S, so Ravi is S + 6. Five years ago: S + 1 = 1.5(S − 5), so S + 1 = 1.5S − 7.5, 0.5S = 8.5 and S = 17. Ravi is 23.
steps: Five years ago: Ravi S + 1, Sunil S − 5
solution.why_others_wrong: 17 is Sunil's age; 29 adds 6 twice; 21 uses S + 6 = 1.5S, ignoring the 5 years.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The sum of the present ages of A and B is 54 years. Eight years from now their ages will be in the ratio 4 : 3. What is B's present age?

solution.concept: Both ages grow by 8, so the future sum is 54 + 16
solution.explanation: In 8 years the sum will be 54 + 16 = 70, split 4 : 3, so A will be 40 and B 30. B's present age = 30 − 8 = 22.
solution.why_others_wrong: 32 is A's present age; 30 is B's age 8 years from now; 24 splits 54 in the ratio 4 : 3 and then subtracts nothing.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average age of a family of five is 28 years. The youngest member is 6 years old. What was the average age of the family just before the youngest member was born?

solution.concept: Go back 6 years: remove the youngest and reduce every other member's age by 6
solution.explanation: Total now = 5 × 28 = 140. Without the youngest, the other four total 134 now. Six years ago each of them was 6 years younger, so their total was 134 − 24 = 110, and the average of the family of four was 110 ÷ 4 = 27.5.
solution.why_others_wrong: 33.5 forgets that the other members were also 6 years younger; 22 subtracts 6 from the average of five; 28 assumes the average does not change.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average of six numbers is 32. Each number is multiplied by 3 and then 5 is added to it. What is the new average?

solution.concept: Multiplying or adding the same amount to every number does the same to the average
solution.explanation: Every number becomes 3x + 5, so the average becomes 3 × 32 + 5 = 101.
solution.why_others_wrong: 96 forgets the + 5; 111 adds 5 before multiplying; 37 only adds 5.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average weight of 20 students is 48 kg. When the teacher's weight is included, the average rises by 1 kg. What is the teacher's weight?

solution.concept: New total − old total = the added weight
solution.explanation: Old total = 20 × 48 = 960 kg. New total = 21 × 49 = 1,029 kg. The teacher weighs 1,029 − 960 = 69 kg.
solution.shortcut: Teacher = new average + (number of students × rise) = 49 + 20 × 1 = 69.
solution.why_others_wrong: 49 kg is the new average; 68 kg adds 20 to the old average; 70 kg adds 21 to the new average.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A grocer mixes 40 kg of rice at ₹52 per kg, 60 kg at ₹45 per kg and some rice at ₹60 per kg. The average cost of the mixture is ₹50 per kg. How many kg of the ₹60 rice did he use?

solution.concept: Weighted average: total cost ÷ total quantity
solution.shortcut: Balance around 50: lot 1 gives +2 × 40 = +80, lot 2 gives −5 × 60 = −300, so the ₹60 rice must give +220 = 10x.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20, 25 and 18 kg leave the mixture's average at about ₹49.8, ₹50.2 and ₹49.7.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average of five consecutive odd numbers is m. If the next three consecutive odd numbers are also included, what is the average of all eight numbers?

solution.concept: Consecutive odd numbers are 2 apart; the average of an evenly spaced list is the middle value
solution.explanation: The five numbers are m − 4, m − 2, m, m + 2, m + 4. The next three are m + 6, m + 8, m + 10. The eight numbers sum to 8m + 24, so the average is m + 3.
solution.shortcut: Eight evenly spaced numbers from m − 4 to m + 10: average = (first + last) ÷ 2 = m + 3.
solution.why_others_wrong: m + 4 averages the first and the eighth wrongly as m and m + 8; m + 6 and m + 5 use the average of the three new numbers alone or forget the first five.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A family's average monthly expenditure was ₹12,000 for the first 5 months of a year, ₹14,500 for the next 4 months and ₹16,000 for the last 3 months. If the family saved ₹26,000 in the whole year, what was its average monthly income?

solution.concept: Annual income = annual expenditure + annual saving; weight each monthly average by its number of months
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹16,333.33 takes the plain average of the three expenditure figures; ₹13,833.33 forgets the savings; ₹15,500 is not supported by any combination of the data.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Kiran buys a used cycle for ₹4,500, spends ₹300 on repairs and sells it for ₹5,400. What is his profit percentage?

solution.concept: Repair costs are part of the cost price
solution.why_others_wrong: 13.33% leaves out the repairs; 11.11% divides by the selling price; 20% takes the profit as ₹900.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The cost price of 15 pens equals the selling price of 12 pens. What is the profit percentage?

solution.concept: Equal amounts of money: compare the number of items
solution.explanation: Let each pen cost ₹1. Then 12 pens sell for ₹15, so the profit on 12 pens is ₹3 on a cost of ₹12, i.e. 25%.
steps: Let CP of 1 pen = 1 ⇒ CP of 15 = 15
solution.why_others_wrong: 20% divides the 3 by 15 instead of 12.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By selling a watch for ₹2,760, a shopkeeper gains 15%. What would be his gain or loss percentage if he sold it for ₹2,280?

solution.concept: Find the cost price first, then compare the new selling price with it
solution.explanation: CP = 2,760 ÷ 1.15 = 2,400. Selling at 2,280 means a loss of 120, which is 120 ÷ 2,400 = 5% of the cost.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5% gain gets the direction wrong; 4.35% divides 120 by 2,760; 20% divides the drop of 480 by 2,400.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A milkman adds 1 litre of water to every 4 litres of milk and sells the mixture at the cost price of milk. What is his gain percentage?

solution.concept: Water costs nothing, so the gain comes from selling 5 litres for the cost of 4
solution.explanation: 4 litres of milk cost him 4 units. He sells 5 litres of mixture at 1 unit each, getting 5 units. Gain = 1 on 4, which is 25%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20% divides the gain by the 5 litres sold instead of the cost of 4 litres.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The profit made by selling an article for ₹1,860 equals the loss made by selling it for ₹1,340. At what price should it be sold to make a profit of 20%?

solution.concept: If profit at S₁ equals loss at S₂, the cost price is midway: (S₁ + S₂) ÷ 2
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,016 starts from 1,680; ₹1,860 already includes a profit of only 16.25%; ₹2,232 adds 20% to 1,860.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The marked price of a sofa is ₹1,500 more than its cost price. When it is sold at a discount of 15%, the shopkeeper makes a profit of ₹600. What is the cost price?

solution.concept: SP = 0.85 × MP and MP = CP + 1,500; profit = SP − CP
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹6,000 is the marked price; ₹4,000 and ₹3,600 give profits of ₹675 and ₹735.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A trader's profit is 25% of his selling price. His cost then rises by 20% while his selling price stays the same. What is his new profit as a percentage of the new cost price?

solution.concept: Profit on SP must be converted to a cost-based figure
solution.explanation: Take SP = 100. Profit = 25, so cost = 75. The new cost = 75 × 1.2 = 90 and the new profit = 10, which is 10 ÷ 90 = 11.11% of the new cost.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5% subtracts 20% from 25%; 10% is profit as a percentage of SP; 8.33% divides 10 by 120.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Rahul sold a scooter to Mohan at a loss of 10%. Mohan spent ₹2,000 on repairs and sold it to Sohan at a profit of 20% on his total cost. If Sohan paid ₹56,400, what did Rahul pay for the scooter?

solution.concept: Work backwards; the repair cost is added to Mohan's cost before his profit
solution.explanation: Mohan's total cost = 56,400 ÷ 1.2 = 47,000. He paid Rahul 47,000 − 2,000 = 45,000, which was 90% of Rahul's cost. So Rahul paid 45,000 ÷ 0.9 = ₹50,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹52,222.22 forgets the repairs; ₹54,444.44 adds them instead of subtracting; ₹47,911.11 takes 20% of the selling price as the profit.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two articles A and B together cost ₹12,000. A is sold at a profit of 15% and B at a loss of 10%, and together they fetch ₹12,480. If A had instead been sold at a loss of 10% and B at a profit of 15%, how much would they have fetched together?

solution.concept: Two unknown costs from the total cost and the total selling price
solution.shortcut: The new total = 2 × 12,000 × 1.025 − 12,480 because each article gets both rates once: 24,600 − 12,480 = 12,120.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹12,480 ignores the swap; ₹11,880 mirrors the gain of 480 into a loss; ₹12,000 assumes the swap cancels.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: An item marked ₹2,500 is sold at a discount of 12%, and the customer gets a further cash discount of ₹50 on the discounted price. How much does the customer pay?

solution.concept: Apply the percentage discount first, then the flat cash discount
solution.explanation: 12% of 2,500 = 300, so the price after discount is 2,200. The cash discount brings it to 2,200 − 50 = ₹2,150.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,156 takes the ₹50 off before the 12%; ₹2,200 ignores the cash discount; ₹2,100 takes ₹100 off.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: After two successive discounts of 20% and x%, an article marked at ₹4,000 is sold for ₹2,720. What is x?

solution.concept: Apply the discounts one after the other; the second is on the reduced price
solution.explanation: After 20%: 4,000 × 0.8 = 3,200. The second discount takes it from 3,200 to 2,720, a cut of 480, which is 480 ÷ 3,200 = 15%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 12% takes 480 as a percentage of 4,000; 32% is the single equivalent discount; 18% has no basis.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If a shopkeeper sells an article at a 20% discount, he gains ₹200. If he sells it at a 30% discount, he loses ₹100. What is the cost price of the article?

solution.concept: The extra 10% discount equals the swing from +200 to −100
solution.explanation: Going from 20% to 30% discount lowers the selling price by 10% of MP and changes the result by 200 + 100 = 300. So MP = 3,000. At 20% off, SP = 2,400, and CP = 2,400 − 200 = ₹2,200.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,400 is the selling price at 20% off; ₹3,000 is the marked price; ₹2,000 uses a swing of 200 only.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A shop allows successive discounts of 20% and 10% on the marked price of a refrigerator and then adds 18% GST on the discounted price. A customer pays ₹16,992. If the shop's profit is 20% of its cost on the pre-tax price, what is the cost price of the refrigerator?

solution.concept: Strip the tax first, then the profit; the marked price is not needed for the cost
solution.explanation: Pre-tax price = 16,992 ÷ 1.18 = 14,400. This is 120% of the cost, so CP = 14,400 ÷ 1.2 = ₹12,000. (The marked price was 14,400 ÷ 0.72 = ₹20,000.)
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹14,160 removes the 20% profit from the tax-inclusive price; ₹14,400 is the pre-tax selling price; ₹11,520 takes 20% off 14,400 instead of dividing by 1.2.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In how many years will ₹4,800 earn a simple interest of ₹1,512 at 6.3% per annum?

solution.concept: SI = P × R × T ÷ 100, so T = SI × 100 ÷ (P × R)
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.5, 6 and 5.5 years give interest of ₹1,360.80, ₹1,814.40 and ₹1,663.20.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The simple interest on a sum for 5 years at 12% per annum is ₹1,200 less than the sum itself. What is the sum?

solution.concept: Interest for 5 years at 12% is 60% of the principal
solution.explanation: SI = 60% of P, so P − 0.6P = 0.4P = 1,200, which gives P = ₹3,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,000 divides 1,200 by 0.6 (taking ₹1,200 as the interest); ₹2,500 and ₹3,600 give differences of ₹1,000 and ₹1,440.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Neha deposits a sum at 8% per annum simple interest. After 2 years she withdraws the interest earned plus ₹5,000 of the principal, and leaves the rest for 3 more years at 10% per annum simple interest. Her total interest over the 5 years is ₹7,700. How much did she deposit?

solution.concept: Split the time into two periods with different principals and rates
solution.explanation: First 2 years: interest = 0.16x. Then the principal is x − 5,000 for 3 years at 10%: interest = 0.3(x − 5,000). So 0.16x + 0.3x − 1,500 = 7,700, giving 0.46x = 9,200 and x = ₹20,000.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What amount will ₹20,000 grow to in 3 years at 5% per annum compound interest, compounded annually?

solution.concept: Amount = P(1 + r/100)ⁿ
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹23,000 is the simple-interest amount; ₹22,050 stops at 2 years; ₹24,310.13 runs to 4 years.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: ₹12,500 is invested at compound interest, compounded annually, at 8% for the first year and 10% for the second year. What is the compound interest for the two years?

solution.concept: With different yearly rates, multiply the year factors: P × 1.08 × 1.10
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,250 is simple interest (8% + 10% of 12,500); ₹2,351.25 averages the rates to 9% for both years.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A sum amounts to ₹8,820 in 1 year at 10% per annum compound interest, compounded half-yearly. What is the sum?

solution.concept: Half-yearly: rate halves (5%) and periods double (2)
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹8,018.18 divides by 1.10 (annual compounding); ₹7,938 subtracts 10% of 8,820; ₹8,400 divides by 1.05 once.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A sum of money doubles itself in 4 years at compound interest, compounded annually. In how many years will it become 8 times itself at the same rate?

solution.concept: At compound interest, equal time periods multiply the sum by the same factor
solution.explanation: Every 4 years the sum doubles. 8 = 2³, so it needs three doublings: 3 × 4 = 12 years.
solution.why_others_wrong: 16 years treats the growth as linear (8 ÷ 2 × 4); 8 years gives only 4 times.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A loan of ₹31,000 at 10% per annum compound interest, compounded annually, is repaid in two annual instalments, the first at the end of year 1 and the second at the end of year 2. The second instalment is twice the first. What is the first instalment?

solution.concept: Loan = sum of the present values of the instalments
solution.explanation: If the first instalment is x, the present values are x ÷ 1.1 and 2x ÷ 1.21. So x(1.1 + 2) ÷ 1.21 = 31,000, which gives 3.1x = 37,510 and x = ₹12,100. The second instalment is ₹24,200.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹10,333.33 ignores interest (31,000 ÷ 3); ₹11,000 is the present value of the first instalment; ₹12,400 adds simple interest for 2 years and splits it 1 : 2.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Meera invests ₹1,00,000 at 10% per annum compound interest, compounded annually. At the end of each year, just after the interest is added, she withdraws ₹20,000. How much remains in the account just after the third withdrawal?

solution.concept: Add interest, then withdraw, year by year: each withdrawal stops earning interest
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹73,100 subtracts all three withdrawals from the full compound amount, as if the withdrawn money kept earning; ₹70,000 uses simple interest; ₹60,280 withdraws before adding interest.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The simple interest on a sum for 3 years at 12% per annum exceeds the compound interest on the same sum for 3 years at 10% per annum, compounded annually, by ₹290. What is the sum?

solution.concept: Express both interests as fractions of P: SI = 36% of P, CI = (1.1³ − 1) = 33.1% of P
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹14,500 uses 30% for the compound interest (simple interest at 10%); ₹12,000 and ₹9,000 give differences of ₹348 and ₹261.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: ₹16,000 grows to ₹19,448.10 in 2 years at compound interest, compounded half-yearly. What is the rate of interest per annum?

solution.concept: Half-yearly: amount = P(1 + r/200)⁴ over 2 years
solution.explanation: 19,448.10 ÷ 16,000 = 1.21550625 = 1.05⁴. So the half-yearly rate is 5% and the annual rate is 10%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5% is the half-yearly rate, not the annual one; 12% and 20% give amounts of ₹20,199.63 and ₹23,425.60.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A invests ₹35,000 for 8 months and B invests ₹40,000 for 6 months in a business. Out of a profit of ₹26,000, what is A's share?

solution.concept: Profit is shared in the ratio of capital × time
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹12,000 is B's share; ₹12,133.33 ignores time (ratio 7 : 8); ₹13,000 splits equally.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A and B invest ₹60,000 and ₹90,000 in a firm. A manages the firm and first takes 20% of the profit as a management fee; the rest is shared in the ratio of their capitals. If A receives ₹2,400 more than B in all, what is the total profit?

solution.concept: Write each partner's total receipt as a fraction of the profit
solution.explanation: Capitals are in the ratio 2 : 3. A gets 0.2P + 2/5 × 0.8P = 0.52P. B gets 3/5 × 0.8P = 0.48P. The difference 0.04P = 2,400, so P = ₹60,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹12,000 treats ₹2,400 as the 20% fee; ₹48,000 is the shared remainder; ₹30,000 halves the answer.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The capitals of A, B and C are in the ratio 3 : 4 : 5, and the periods for which they invest are in the ratio 4 : 3 : 2. Out of a profit of ₹51,000, what is C's share?

solution.concept: Profit ratio = capital ratio × time ratio, term by term
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹21,250 uses capitals only (5/12); ₹18,000 and ₹12,750 split by time only or by 1/4.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A and B invest ₹80,000 and ₹50,000 in a partnership. Under their agreement, each partner first receives interest on capital at 10% per annum, and the profit left after that is shared equally. If the profit for the year is ₹43,000, how much does A receive in all?

solution.concept: Apply the agreement in its order: interest on capital first, then the remainder
solution.explanation: Interest on capital: A gets 8,000 and B gets 5,000. Remaining profit = 43,000 − 13,000 = 30,000, shared equally, so 15,000 each. A receives 8,000 + 15,000 = ₹23,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹26,461.54 shares the whole profit in the capital ratio 8 : 5; ₹21,500 shares it equally; ₹20,000 is B's total.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two vessels contain milk and water in the ratios 3 : 1 and 5 : 3. Equal quantities from the two vessels are mixed. What is the ratio of milk to water in the new mixture?

solution.concept: Convert each ratio to a fraction of the vessel's contents, then add equal volumes
solution.explanation: Take 1 litre from each. Milk = 3/4 + 5/8 = 11/8 litres; water = 1/4 + 3/8 = 5/8 litres. Ratio = 11 : 5.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 : 1 adds the ratio terms (8 : 4), which is wrong because one vessel's ratio has 4 parts and the other 8; 5 : 3 is the second vessel alone; 4 : 1 has no basis.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A container holds 60 litres of pure milk. 6 litres are taken out and replaced with water. Then 10 litres of the mixture are taken out and replaced with water. How much milk is now in the container?

solution.concept: Each replacement leaves the milk fraction multiplied by (1 − removed/total)
solution.explanation: After the first step the milk is 54 litres out of 60. Removing 10 litres of the mixture removes 10/60 of the milk, so 54 × 50/60 = 45 litres remain.
solution.why_others_wrong: 44 L assumes the second 10 litres were pure milk; 48.6 L removes 6 litres both times; 50 L subtracts only the second removal.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A dealer mixes two varieties of pulses costing ₹80 and ₹95 per kg in the ratio 2 : 3. At what price per kg must he sell the mixture to gain 20%?

solution.concept: Weighted average cost, then add the profit
solution.explanation: Cost of 5 kg = 2 × 80 + 3 × 95 = 445, so the cost is ₹89 per kg. For a 20% gain, SP = 89 × 1.2 = ₹106.80.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹105 uses the simple average 87.5; ₹103.20 reverses the ratio (cost 86); ₹89 is the cost without profit.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: 40 litres of a salt solution contain 15% salt. How many litres of water must be evaporated to make the solution 25% salt?

solution.concept: Evaporation removes only water: the amount of salt stays fixed
solution.explanation: Salt = 15% of 40 = 6 litres. For 6 litres to be 25% of the solution, the solution must be 24 litres. So 40 − 24 = 16 litres of water must be evaporated.
solution.why_others_wrong: 24 L is the volume left, not the water removed; 10 L uses (25 − 15)% of 40; 15 L has no basis.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Three vessels hold 30 litres, 40 litres and 50 litres of milk–water mixtures in the ratios 2 : 1, 3 : 5 and 7 : 3 respectively. All three are poured into one drum. What is the ratio of milk to water in the drum?

solution.concept: Find the actual litres of milk in each vessel and add
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 : 3 adds the ratio terms (12 : 9), ignoring the different volumes; 5 : 7 is inverted; 3 : 2 averages the fractions.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A 60-litre container is full of milk and water in the ratio 3 : 1. How much of the mixture must be drawn off and replaced with water so that the container holds equal amounts of milk and water?

solution.concept: Only the milk fraction falls during replacement; the total stays 60 litres
solution.explanation: Milk is 45 litres. After drawing off x litres, milk = 45 × (60 − x)/60. For a 1 : 1 mixture, milk must be 30 litres: 45(60 − x)/60 = 30, so 60 − x = 40 and x = 20 litres.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15 L is the water already present; 30 L is the water you would add without drawing anything off (and the container would overflow); 22.5 L assumes pure milk is drawn off and halves the milk.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A is 25% more efficient than B. B alone can finish a job in 20 days. In how many days can A and B together finish it?

solution.concept: Efficiency is work per day; 25% more efficient means 1.25 times the daily work
solution.explanation: B does 1/20 of the job a day, so A does 1.25/20 = 1/16. Together: 1/20 + 1/16 = 9/80 per day, so the job takes 80/9 = 8 8/9 days.
solution.why_others_wrong: 16 days is A alone; 10 days assumes A and B are equally fast; 9 days rounds 80/9.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A job can be finished by 4 men in 26 days, or by 6 women in 26 days, or by 8 children in 26 days. In how many days can 1 man, 1 woman and 1 child working together finish it?

solution.concept: Find each person's daily share of the job
solution.explanation: One man does 1/104 of the job a day, one woman 1/156 and one child 1/208. Together: 6/624 + 4/624 + 3/624 = 13/624 = 1/48. So they take 48 days.
solution.why_others_wrong: 52 days counts the trio as only 2 men; 39 days treats them as 2⅔ men; 36 days has no basis.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A, B and C can finish a job alone in 10, 15 and 30 days respectively. They start together, but A leaves 2 days before the job is finished and B leaves 3 days before it is finished. In how many days is the job finished?

solution.concept: Let the total be t days: A works t − 2 days, B t − 3 days and C all t days
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 days is the time if all three worked throughout; 8 and 6 days do not make the work add up to 1.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 10 hours and 15 hours, and pipe C can empty the full tank in 20 hours. If all three are opened together on the empty tank, in how many hours will it be full?

solution.concept: Add filling rates and subtract emptying rates
solution.explanation: Net rate = 1/10 + 1/15 − 1/20 = 6/60 + 4/60 − 3/60 = 7/60 of the tank per hour. Time = 60/7 = 8 4/7 hours.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 hours ignores pipe C; 12 hours takes the net rate as 1/12; 10 hours ignores pipe B and C.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: An inlet pipe can fill a tank in 6 hours. When the tank is half full, an outlet pipe that can empty the full tank in 9 hours is also opened. How long does it take to fill the tank completely, starting from empty?

solution.concept: Split the filling into two stages with different net rates
solution.explanation: The first half takes 3 hours. Then the net rate is 1/6 − 1/9 = 1/18 per hour, so the second half takes (1/2) ÷ (1/18) = 9 hours. Total = 12 hours.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9 hours is the second stage alone; 18 hours runs both pipes from the start; 10.5 hours adds 3 hours to half of the 15 hours the second stage would take from empty.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 12 hours and 15 hours respectively. They are opened alternately for one hour each, starting with A, on an empty tank. How long will it take to fill the tank?

solution.concept: Find the work done in each 2-hour cycle, then finish the last part carefully
solution.explanation: One cycle (A then B) fills 1/12 + 1/15 = 9/60 = 3/20. After 6 cycles (12 hours) 18/20 is full, leaving 1/10. In the 13th hour A fills 1/12, leaving 1/10 − 1/12 = 1/60. B fills 1/60 in (1/60) ÷ (1/15) = 1/4 hour. Total = 13 hours 15 minutes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 13 h 20 min gives B 1/3 hour for the last 1/60 (as if B filled the tank in 20 hours); 13 h 30 min and 14 hours round the last part up.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A car travels for 2 hours at 45 km/h and then for 3 hours at 60 km/h. What is its average speed for the whole journey?

solution.concept: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time
solution.explanation: Distance = 2 × 45 + 3 × 60 = 90 + 180 = 270 km in 5 hours, so the average speed is 54 km/h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 52.5 km/h averages the two speeds without weighting by time; 55 and 50 km/h use 275 or 250 km.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A police jeep chases a car that is 600 m ahead on the same road. The jeep runs at 72 km/h and the car at 54 km/h. How long will the jeep take to catch the car?

solution.concept: Same direction: relative speed = difference of speeds; convert km/h to m/s with × 5/18
solution.explanation: Relative speed = 72 − 54 = 18 km/h = 18 × 5/18 = 5 m/s. Time = 600 ÷ 5 = 120 seconds = 2 minutes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 33⅓ seconds divides 600 by 18 without converting units; 17.14 seconds adds the speeds; 1 minute halves the time.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two friends start at the same time from towns A and B, 30 km apart, and walk towards each other at 4 km/h and 6 km/h respectively. How far from A do they meet?

solution.concept: Towards each other: relative speed = sum of speeds; each walks for the same time
solution.explanation: They close the gap at 4 + 6 = 10 km/h, so they meet after 30 ÷ 10 = 3 hours. The friend from A has walked 4 × 3 = 12 km.
solution.shortcut: The distance splits in the ratio of speeds 4 : 6, so A's part = 30 × 4/10 = 12 km.
solution.why_others_wrong: 18 km is the distance from B; 15 km assumes equal speeds; 10 km is the distance covered in one hour.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A car goes up a hill road at 30 km/h and comes back down the same road at 60 km/h. The round trip takes 6 hours. How long is the road one way?

solution.concept: Time up + time down = total time
solution.shortcut: The average speed for the round trip is 2 × 30 × 60 ÷ 90 = 40 km/h, so the round trip is 240 km.
solution.why_others_wrong: 135 km uses the simple average 45 km/h; 90 km and 180 km use 30 km/h or 60 km/h for the whole trip.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two runners start together from the same point on a 400 m circular track and run in opposite directions at 6 m/s and 4 m/s. After how many seconds will they meet for the third time?

solution.concept: Opposite directions on a loop: they meet each time they jointly cover one full lap
solution.explanation: Together they cover 6 + 4 = 10 m every second, so they meet every 400 ÷ 10 = 40 seconds. The third meeting is at 3 × 40 = 120 seconds.
solution.why_others_wrong: 40 s is the first meeting; 200 s is when they are next together at the start; 600 s uses the same-direction speed 2 m/s.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A car would take 2 hours less to cover 480 km if its speed were 8 km/h more. What is its usual speed?

solution.concept: Set up time at the usual speed minus time at the faster speed
solution.explanation: 480/v − 480/(v + 8) = 2. This gives 480 × 8 = 2v(v + 8), i.e. v² + 8v − 1,920 = 0 = (v − 40)(v + 48). So v = 40 km/h (speed is positive).
steps: Check: 12 hours at 40 km/h, 10 hours at 48 km/h
solution.why_others_wrong: 48 km/h is the faster speed; 32 and 36 km/h give time savings of 3 hours and about 2.4 hours.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A boat goes downstream at 20 km/h and upstream at 12 km/h. What is the speed of the stream?

solution.concept: Stream speed = (downstream − upstream) ÷ 2
solution.explanation: Downstream = b + s = 20 and upstream = b − s = 12. Subtracting, 2s = 8, so s = 4 km/h (and b = 16 km/h).
solution.why_others_wrong: 8 km/h forgets to halve; 16 km/h is the boat's speed in still water.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A boat's speed in still water is 12 km/h and the stream flows at 2 km/h. How long will the boat take to go 35 km upstream?

solution.concept: Upstream speed = boat speed − stream speed
solution.explanation: Upstream speed = 12 − 2 = 10 km/h, so 35 km takes 3.5 hours = 3 hours 30 minutes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 hours 30 minutes uses the downstream speed 14 km/h; 2 hours 55 minutes ignores the stream.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A motorboat whose speed in still water is 20 km/h goes 48 km downstream and comes back in a total of 5 hours. What is the speed of the stream?

solution.concept: Total time = d/(b + s) + d/(b − s)
solution.why_others_wrong: 5, 3 and 2 km/h give round-trip times of about 5.12, 4.91 and 4.85 hours.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A boat's speed in still water is 10 km/h and the stream flows at 2 km/h. It goes downstream from A to B and then comes back upstream to C, the midpoint of AB. The whole trip takes 7 hours. What is the distance AB?

solution.concept: Downstream for the full distance, upstream for half of it
solution.explanation: Downstream speed = 12 km/h and upstream speed = 8 km/h. d/12 + (d/2)/8 = 7, so d/12 + d/16 = 7, 7d/48 = 7 and d = 48 km.
solution.why_others_wrong: 42 km and 56 km give 6.1 and 8.2 hours; 36 km gives 5.25 hours.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A boat's upstream speed is 60% of its downstream speed. It goes 30 km upstream and returns to its starting point in 8 hours. What is the speed of the boat in still water?

solution.concept: Write both speeds with one unknown; still-water speed = (down + up) ÷ 2
solution.explanation: Let downstream speed be d; upstream is 0.6d. 30/(0.6d) + 30/d = 8 gives 50/d + 30/d = 80/d = 8, so d = 10 km/h and upstream = 6 km/h. Still-water speed = (10 + 6) ÷ 2 = 8 km/h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 km/h is the downstream speed and 6 km/h the upstream speed; 9 km/h has no basis.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A train 150 m long crosses a signal pole in 9 seconds. What is its speed in km/h?

solution.concept: Crossing a pole: distance = length of the train; m/s × 18/5 = km/h
solution.why_others_wrong: 54 and 72 km/h use 15 or 20 m/s; 50 km/h uses × 3 instead of × 3.6.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A train crosses a 180 m long bridge in 15 seconds and a 330 m long tunnel in 21 seconds at the same speed. What is the length of the train?

solution.concept: The extra length (330 − 180) takes the extra time (21 − 15)
solution.explanation: The extra 150 m takes 6 seconds, so the speed is 25 m/s. In 15 seconds the train covers 375 m = its length + 180, so its length is 195 m.
solution.why_others_wrong: 150 m is the difference in the lengths of the tunnel and the bridge; 225 m and 175 m give different speeds for the bridge and the tunnel (225 m: 27 m/s and 26.4 m/s).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two trains 200 m and 160 m long run on parallel tracks in the same direction at 72 km/h and 54 km/h. How long will the faster train take to pass the slower one completely?

solution.concept: Same direction: relative speed = difference; distance = sum of lengths
solution.explanation: Relative speed = 72 − 54 = 18 km/h = 5 m/s. The faster train must gain 200 + 160 = 360 m, which takes 360 ÷ 5 = 72 seconds.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10.29 seconds adds the speeds (opposite directions); 20 seconds uses 360 ÷ 18 without converting; 36 seconds uses only half the combined length.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two trains 260 m and 240 m long run on parallel tracks. They cross each other completely in 10 seconds when moving in opposite directions and in 50 seconds when moving in the same direction. What is the speed of the faster train in km/h?

solution.concept: Opposite directions give the sum of speeds; same direction gives the difference
solution.explanation: Total length = 500 m. Sum of speeds = 500 ÷ 10 = 50 m/s; difference = 500 ÷ 50 = 10 m/s. The faster train's speed = (50 + 10) ÷ 2 = 30 m/s = 108 km/h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 72 km/h is the slower train (20 m/s); 90 km/h uses the average 25 m/s; 126 km/h uses 35 m/s.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A square field has an area of 2,025 m². What is the cost of fencing it all round at ₹15 per metre?

solution.concept: Side of a square = √area; fencing runs along the perimeter
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹675 fences one side only; ₹1,350 two sides; ₹30,375 multiplies the area by the rate.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How much liquid can a hemispherical bowl of internal radius 10.5 cm hold? (Use π = 22/7.)

solution.concept: Volume of a hemisphere = (2/3)πr³
solution.why_others_wrong: 4,851 cm³ is the full sphere; 1,212.75 cm³ is a quarter-sphere; 3,638.25 cm³ forgets the 2/3.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The length, breadth and height of a cuboid are in the ratio 4 : 3 : 2, and its total surface area is 1,872 cm². What is its volume?

solution.concept: TSA of a cuboid = 2(lb + bh + hl); write each side as a multiple of k
solution.explanation: With sides 4k, 3k, 2k: TSA = 2(12k² + 6k² + 8k²) = 52k² = 1,872, so k² = 36 and k = 6. The sides are 24, 18 and 12 cm, and the volume is 24 × 18 × 12 = 5,184 cm³.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2,592 cm³ is half the volume; 1,728 cm³ is 12³; 6,912 cm³ uses a height of 16 cm.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A solid cylinder has a base radius of 6 cm and a height of 15 cm. A cone of the same base radius and height 8 cm is hollowed out from one end. What is the total surface area of the remaining solid?

solution.concept: Count every exposed surface: the cylinder's curved surface, the uncut base, and the inside of the cone (its curved surface); the cut base is gone
solution.explanation: Curved surface of the cylinder = 2π × 6 × 15 = 180π. The intact base = π × 6² = 36π. The cone's slant height = √(6² + 8²) = 10, so its curved surface = π × 6 × 10 = 60π. Total = 180π + 36π + 60π = 276π cm².
steps: Bottom base = 36π (the top base is removed)
solution.why_others_wrong: 312π also counts the removed top base; 240π leaves out the bottom base; 216π ignores the hollow cone.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the product of the two numbers is a perfect square?

solution.concept: List the favourable outcomes among the 36 equally likely pairs
solution.explanation: Products that are perfect squares: doubles (1,1), (2,2), …, (6,6) give 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36 (6 outcomes), and (1,4) and (4,1) give 4. That is 8 outcomes, so P = 8/36 = 2/9.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/6 counts only the doubles; 7/36 counts (1, 4) but not (4, 1).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: One card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled pack of 52 cards. What is the probability that it is a red card bearing a number from 2 to 10?

solution.concept: Count the favourable cards: 9 numbered cards in each red suit
solution.explanation: Each red suit (hearts and diamonds) has the numbered cards 2 to 10, which is 9 cards. So 18 cards are favourable and P = 18/52 = 9/26.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9/13 counts numbered cards of all four suits; 5/13 includes the red aces; 1/2 counts every red card.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A bag contains 5 red and 7 blue balls. Two balls are drawn one after the other without replacement. What is the probability that the second ball is red?

solution.concept: Total probability over the colour of the first ball (or symmetry: every position is equally likely to hold any ball)
solution.shortcut: Without any information about the first ball, the second is like a fresh draw: 5/12.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5/11 assumes the first ball was blue; 4/11 assumes it was red; 35/132 is only the blue-then-red case.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Three fair coins are tossed and a fair die is rolled. What is the probability of getting exactly two heads and an even number on the die?

solution.concept: Independent events: multiply their probabilities
solution.explanation: P(exactly two heads) = 3/8 (HHT, HTH, THH out of 8). P(even) = 1/2. P(both) = 3/8 × 1/2 = 3/16.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3/8 ignores the die; 1/4 uses P(two heads) = 1/2; 7/16 adds the probabilities instead of multiplying.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two cards are drawn together at random from a well-shuffled pack of 52 cards. What is the probability that both are kings or both are red?

solution.concept: Addition rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B)
solution.explanation: Total pairs = C(52, 2) = 1,326. Both kings: C(4, 2) = 6. Both red: C(26, 2) = 325. Both red kings: 1 (the king of hearts and the king of diamonds). Favourable = 6 + 325 − 1 = 330, so P = 330/1,326 = 55/221.
solution.why_others_wrong: 331/1,326 adds 6 + 325 without removing the pair of red kings counted twice; 25/102 is 'both red' alone; 1/221 is 'both kings' alone.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Bag A contains 4 red and 6 green balls; bag B contains 7 red and 3 green balls. A fair coin is tossed: on heads bag A is chosen, on tails bag B. Two balls are then drawn together from the chosen bag. What is the probability that both balls are red?

solution.concept: Total probability: weight each bag's probability by the chance of choosing it
solution.why_others_wrong: 3/5 forgets the ½ for choosing a bag; 13/40 draws with replacement; 2/15 uses bag A only.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In how many different ways can the letters of the word RUPEE be arranged?

solution.concept: Arrangements with a repeated letter: n! ÷ (repeats)!
solution.explanation: RUPEE has 5 letters with E twice. Arrangements = 5! ÷ 2! = 120 ÷ 2 = 60.
solution.why_others_wrong: 120 treats the two Es as different; 30 divides by 4; 24 is 4!.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A bag contains 5 red and 4 white balls. In how many ways can 3 balls be selected so that at least one of them is white?

solution.concept: 'At least one' = all selections − selections with none
solution.explanation: All selections of 3 from 9 = C(9, 3) = 84. Selections with no white ball = C(5, 3) = 10. So 84 − 10 = 74.
solution.why_others_wrong: 84 is every selection; 64 subtracts 20; 80 subtracts only C(4, 3) = 4 (the all-white selections).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many four-digit even numbers can be formed with the digits 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 if no digit is repeated?

solution.concept: Fill the restricted places first; treat the case of 0 in the units place separately
solution.explanation: Units digit 0: the other three places can be filled in 6 × 5 × 4 = 120 ways. Units digit 2, 4 or 6: the thousands digit cannot be 0 or the units digit, so 5 choices, then 5 and 4: 3 × 5 × 5 × 4 = 300. Total = 420.
solution.why_others_wrong: 360 counts all four even digits the same way (4 × 90); 480 allows 0 in the thousands place; 400 has no basis.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In how many ways can the letters of the word SAVINGS be arranged so that the two S's are not next to each other?

solution.concept: Not together = total arrangements − arrangements with the S's together
solution.explanation: SAVINGS has 7 letters with S twice: total = 7! ÷ 2! = 2,520. Treating SS as one block gives 6 units, all different: 6! = 720. So 2,520 − 720 = 1,800.
solution.shortcut: Gap method: arrange A, V, I, N, G in 5! = 120 ways, then put the two S's in 2 of the 6 gaps: C(6, 2) = 15. 120 × 15 = 1,800.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2,520 ignores the condition; 720 counts the S's together; 2,160 subtracts only 360.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the total rooftop solar capacity installed in Q3 by the five districts together?

solution.concept: Column total
solution.why_others_wrong: 2,165 kW is the Q2 total; the other two are addition slips.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Churu's installation in Q4 was what percentage more than its installation in Q1?

solution.concept: Percentage more = increase ÷ earlier value × 100
solution.explanation: Churu installed 280 kW in Q1 and 455 kW in Q4. The increase of 175 kW is 175 ÷ 280 = 62.5% of the Q1 figure.
solution.why_others_wrong: 38.46% divides by the Q4 figure; 162.5% is Q4 as a percentage of Q1; 60% is a rounding guess.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the ratio of the Q2 installations of Alwar and Bikaner together to the Q3 installations of Churu and Jhunjhunu together?

solution.concept: Add the two cells on each side, then reduce
solution.explanation: Q2 of Alwar and Bikaner = 515 + 440 = 955. Q3 of Churu and Jhunjhunu = 390 + 445 = 835. 955 : 835 = 191 : 167 (dividing by 5).
solution.why_others_wrong: 167 : 191 is reversed; 8 : 7 and 19 : 17 are close but not equal to 955 : 835.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In how many of the five districts was the Q4 installation more than 30% of that district's installation for the whole year?

solution.concept: Compare each Q4 value with 30% of the row total
solution.explanation: Row totals and 30% of them: Alwar 2,040 → 612 (Q4 625, yes); Bikaner 1,880 → 564 (575, yes); Churu 1,460 → 438 (455, yes); Dausa 2,195 → 658.5 (655, no); Jhunjhunu 1,720 → 516 (540, yes). So 4 districts.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 misses that Dausa falls just short (655 against 658.5); 3 and 2 drop districts that are only slightly above 30%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In Q1 of 2026-27, every district except Dausa installs 20% more than it did in Q4 of 2025-26, while Dausa installs 10% less than its Q4 figure. What is the total installation of the five districts in Q1 of 2026-27?

solution.concept: Apply each district's own change to its Q4 value
solution.explanation: The four districts other than Dausa installed 2,850 − 655 = 2,195 kW in Q4; 20% more is 2,634 kW. Dausa's 655 kW falls 10% to 589.5 kW. Total = 2,634 + 589.5 = 3,223.5 kW.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3,420 kW applies +20% to Dausa too; 3,354.5 kW subtracts only 10% of Dausa from 3,420; 2,565 kW applies −10% to every district.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many parcels did Hub C deliver on the next day?

solution.concept: Next-day deliveries are a percentage of the parcels left after the same day, not of all parcels
solution.explanation: Hub C delivered 58% of 15,000 = 8,700 on the same day, leaving 6,300. 85% of 6,300 = 5,355 were delivered the next day.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6,300 is the number left after the same day; 7,395 takes 85% of 8,700; 945 is the number delayed.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Which hub delivered the largest number of parcels on the same day?

solution.concept: Compare numbers, not percentages: same-day count = parcels × same-day %
solution.explanation: Same-day deliveries: A 7,800, B 7,200, C 8,700, D 6,720 and E 7,560. Hub C is the largest even though its percentage (58%) is the lowest.
solution.why_others_wrong: Hub D has the highest percentage but the fewest same-day parcels; Hub A and Hub E come second and third.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What percentage of the parcels received at Hub D were delivered within two days (on the same day or the next day)?

solution.concept: Delivered within two days = same day + next day; the next-day percentage applies to the remainder only
solution.explanation: Same day: 80% of 8,400 = 6,720. Remainder 1,680, of which 75% = 1,260 were delivered the next day. Within two days: 7,980 of 8,400 = 95%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 77.5% averages 80 and 75; 60% multiplies them; 85% adds only 5 points for the next day.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The number of delayed parcels at Hub E is what percentage of the number of delayed parcels at Hub B?

solution.concept: Delayed = received × (1 − same-day %) × (1 − next-day %)
solution.why_others_wrong: 80% is how much more E has, not the percentage; 55.56% is B as a percentage of E; 135% compares the parcels left after the same day (3,240 and 2,400).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If Hub C had delivered 70% of its parcels on the same day, and the same next-day percentage had applied to the rest, how many more parcels would it have delivered within two days?

solution.concept: A higher same-day share leaves fewer parcels for the next day; compute both stages again
solution.explanation: New same-day = 10,500 and new remainder 4,500, of which 85% = 3,825 go the next day. Within two days: 14,325 instead of 8,700 + 5,355 = 14,055. Increase = 270.
solution.shortcut: Only the extra 12% (1,800 parcels) changes stage, and 85% of them would have gone the next day anyway: 1,800 × 15% = 270.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,800 ignores the fall in next-day deliveries; 1,530 is that fall itself; 945 is the old number delayed.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many saplings did Bharati and Disha plant together?

solution.concept: Read the two bars and add
solution.explanation: Bharati planted 360 and Disha 300, so together 660.
solution.why_others_wrong: 720 doubles Bharati; 600 doubles Disha; 780 uses Gyanodaya (420) instead of Disha.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Eklavya planted what percentage more saplings than Ashoka?

solution.concept: Percentage more = difference ÷ the value after 'than' × 100
solution.explanation: Eklavya 600, Ashoka 480. The difference 120 is 120 ÷ 480 = 25% of Ashoka's figure.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20% divides by Eklavya's 600; 125% is Eklavya as a percentage of Ashoka.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the ratio of the saplings planted by Chanakya and Gyanodaya together to those planted by Bharati and Disha together?

solution.concept: Sum each pair, then reduce
solution.explanation: Chanakya + Gyanodaya = 540 + 420 = 960. Bharati + Disha = 360 + 300 = 660. 960 : 660 = 16 : 11.
solution.why_others_wrong: 11 : 16 is reversed; 8 : 5 and 32 : 21 come from misreading one bar by 60.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: 90% of Ashoka's saplings, 85% of Eklavya's and 80% of Chanakya's survived. How many saplings of these three schools survived in all?

solution.concept: Apply each school's own survival rate to its own bar
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,377 applies the average rate 85% to the combined 1,620; 1,620 counts every sapling; 1,296 uses 80% for all.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What percentage of all the orders received by the five outlets were online?

solution.concept: Share = online total ÷ (online + walk-in) total
solution.why_others_wrong: 44% is the walk-in share; 50% and 58% are slips in one of the totals.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: At which outlet did online orders form the largest share of the outlet's own orders?

solution.concept: Compare online ÷ total for each outlet
solution.explanation: Online shares: Spice Hub 640/1,050 ≈ 61.0%, Tandoor Tales 48%, Curry Leaf 720/1,050 ≈ 68.6%, Biryani Bay 585/900 = 65% and Dosa Point 37.5%. Curry Leaf is highest.
solution.why_others_wrong: Biryani Bay is second (65%); Spice Hub has many online orders but also many walk-ins.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Online orders at Curry Leaf were what percentage more than online orders at Dosa Point?

solution.concept: Percentage more = difference ÷ smaller (base) value × 100
solution.explanation: Curry Leaf 720, Dosa Point 375. Difference 345, and 345 ÷ 375 = 92%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 47.92% divides by 720; 192% is Curry Leaf as a percentage of Dosa Point.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Online orders average ₹350 each and walk-in orders ₹420 each. The delivery platform keeps a 20% commission on the value of online orders. What was Tandoor Tales' net revenue for the week?

solution.concept: Commission applies to online value only
solution.explanation: Online value = 480 × 350 = 1,68,000; after 20% commission the outlet keeps 1,34,400. Walk-in value = 520 × 420 = 2,18,400. Net revenue = 1,34,400 + 2,18,400 = ₹3,52,800.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹3,86,400 ignores the commission; ₹3,09,120 deducts it from walk-in sales too; ₹3,40,800 swaps the two average values.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How much of the budget is allocated to water supply?

solution.concept: Amount = angle ÷ 360 × total
solution.explanation: Each degree stands for 720 ÷ 360 = ₹2 crore. Water supply has 72°, so it gets 72 × 2 = ₹144 crore.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹72 crore reads the angle as crore; ₹180 crore uses Roads (90°); ₹120 crore uses 60°.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What percentage of the budget goes to health?

solution.concept: Percentage = angle ÷ 360 × 100
solution.explanation: Health has 45°, which is 45 ÷ 360 = 1/8 = 12.5% of the budget.
solution.why_others_wrong: 45% reads the angle as a percentage; 15% and 10% use 54° or 36°.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By how much does the allocation for roads exceed the combined allocation for sanitation and street lighting?

solution.concept: Subtract angles first, then convert
solution.explanation: Roads 90° against Sanitation + Street lighting = 54° + 27° = 81°. The gap is 9°, worth 9 × 2 = ₹18 crore.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹9 crore leaves the gap in degrees; ₹36 crore and ₹27 crore use 18° or 13.5°.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The education allocation is raised by 25%, and the extra money is taken entirely from 'Others', keeping the total budget the same. What will be the central angle of 'Others'?

solution.concept: Work in rupees (or directly in degrees): 25% of Education's 36° is 9°
solution.explanation: Education gets 36° = ₹72 crore; 25% more is ₹18 crore = 9°. 'Others' falls from 36° to 36° − 9° = 27°.
solution.why_others_wrong: 45° adds the 9° instead of subtracting; 18° takes off 18 degrees (reading crore as degrees); 36° leaves 'Others' unchanged.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Next year the total budget rises by 15% and health's share of the budget rises to 15%. By what percentage does the health allocation increase?

solution.concept: New amount = new total × new share; compare with the old amount
solution.explanation: This year health gets ₹90 crore (12.5% of 720). Next year the budget is 720 × 1.15 = ₹828 crore and health gets 15% of it = ₹124.2 crore. Increase = 34.2 ÷ 90 = 38%.
solution.shortcut: Growth factor = 1.15 (budget) × 15/12.5 (share) = 1.15 × 1.2 = 1.38.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20% counts only the change in share; 15% only the budget growth; 32.25% treats the share as rising by 15% of itself.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many women visited the fair on Day 3?

solution.concept: Use the women's chart and the women's total
solution.explanation: Day 3 has 25% of the 24,000 women visitors: 24,000 × 0.25 = 6,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: 13,200 is all visitors on Day 3; 5,400 is women on Day 4; 7,200 is men on Day 3.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many men visited the fair on Day 4?

solution.concept: Men on a day = all visitors that day − women that day
solution.why_others_wrong: 5,400 is the women; 15,000 is everyone; 9,000 takes 25% of the 36,000 men, which the charts do not give.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: On which day did women form the largest share of that day's visitors?

solution.concept: For each day, divide women by all visitors
solution.why_others_wrong: Day 2 is a close second; Day 4 has the most visitors but a low women's share.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The entry ticket costs ₹120, and women get a 25% discount on it. What was the ticket revenue on Day 4?

solution.concept: Split Day 4's visitors into men and women and price each group
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹18,00,000 ignores the discount; ₹13,50,000 gives everyone the discount; ₹15,12,000 gives the discount to the men instead.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By what percentage did generation rise from March to April?

solution.concept: Percentage change = change ÷ earlier value × 100
solution.explanation: March 52 MU, April 65 MU. The rise of 13 MU is 13 ÷ 52 = 25% of March's figure.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20% divides by April's 65; 13% is the rise in MU, not a percentage.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the ratio of the total generation in January–March to the total generation in April–June?

solution.concept: Add each quarter's three months, then reduce
solution.explanation: January–March = 40 + 46 + 52 = 138 MU. April–June = 65 + 78 + 79 = 222 MU. 138 : 222 = 23 : 37 (dividing by 6).
solution.why_others_wrong: 37 : 23 is reversed; 2 : 3 is close but not exact; 46 : 79 compares February with June.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The farm sells the first 50 MU it generates in a month at ₹3.20 per unit and any further units that month at ₹2.80 per unit. What was its revenue for May? (1 MU = 10 lakh units.)

solution.concept: Slab pricing: price each slab separately
solution.explanation: May generation = 78 MU. First 50 MU × ₹3.20 = ₹160 million; the other 28 MU × ₹2.80 = ₹78.4 million. Total = ₹238.4 million = ₹23.84 crore.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹24.96 crore prices all 78 MU at ₹3.20; ₹21.84 crore prices all at ₹2.80; ₹23.40 crore uses a flat ₹3.00.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many flights in all did the airport handle in 2023?

solution.concept: Add the two lines' values for the year; the unit is thousands
solution.explanation: 2023: domestic 54 thousand + international 15 thousand = 69 thousand = 69,000 flights.
solution.why_others_wrong: 54,000 counts only domestic flights; 75,000 uses 2024's domestic figure (60 + 15); 66,000 is 2023's domestic plus 2022's international (54 + 12).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What percentage of all flights handled in 2025 were international?

solution.concept: Share = part ÷ (domestic + international) × 100
solution.explanation: 2025: international 21 thousand out of 63 + 21 = 84 thousand, which is 25%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 33.33% divides by domestic flights only; 21% reads the value as a percentage.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In 2026 domestic flights grow by 10% and international flights by 20% over 2025. What percentage of all 2026 flights will be international?

solution.concept: Project both lines, then take the share
solution.explanation: 2026: domestic 63 × 1.1 = 69.3 thousand, international 21 × 1.2 = 25.2 thousand. Share = 25.2 ÷ 94.5 = 26⅔%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 28% and 30% add percentage points to the 2025 share; 25.2% divides by 100 instead of 94.5.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many dupattas did the cooperative produce?

solution.concept: Split the non-saree items in the ratio dupattas : stoles = 1.5 : 1 = 3 : 2
solution.explanation: Sarees = 40% of 1,200 = 480, so dupattas + stoles = 720. Dupattas : stoles = 3 : 2, so dupattas = 3/5 × 720 = 432.
solution.why_others_wrong: 288 is the stoles; 360 splits 720 equally; 480 is the sarees.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the cooperative's revenue from the sarees sold in October?

solution.concept: Revenue = units sold × selling price
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹11,52,000 counts all 480 sarees; ₹7,34,400 uses the production cost; ₹9,60,000 uses 400 sarees.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many items in all remained unsold at the end of October?

solution.concept: Unsold = produced − sold, for each item
solution.explanation: Unsold sarees = 72, dupattas = 108, stoles = 36. Total = 216.
solution.why_others_wrong: 180 leaves out the stoles; 252 is the number of stoles sold; 144 halves the dupattas.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What percentage of all the items produced were sold?

solution.concept: Use actual numbers sold; the three percentages apply to different bases
solution.explanation: Items sold = 408 + 324 + 252 = 984, out of 1,200, which is 82%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 82.5% averages 85%, 75% and 87.5% without weighting; 18% is the unsold share.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Taking profit as the revenue from items sold minus the production cost of all items produced, what was the cooperative's profit on dupattas in October?

solution.concept: The cost of unsold items still counts against the revenue
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹71,280 counts the cost of only the dupattas sold; ₹95,040 assumes all were sold; ₹23,040 is a slip in the cost.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many runners finished the 10 km race?

solution.concept: Finishers = registrations × finishing percentage
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,800 is all registrations; 180 is the non-finishers; 1,710 uses 95%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the total entry-fee collection from all registered runners?

solution.concept: Fee income = Σ registrations × fee
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹82,50,000 multiplies 6,000 runners by the plain average fee; ₹54,06,000 counts finishers only; ₹60,60,000 is an addition slip.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Women made up what percentage of all registered runners?

solution.concept: Weight each category's percentage by its registrations
solution.why_others_wrong: 32.5% is the simple average of the four percentages.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the organisers' fee collection minus the cost of the medals?

solution.concept: Medals go to finishers only
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹48,60,000 buys medals for all 6,000 runners; ₹40,71,000 counts fees from finishers only; ₹13,35,000 is the medal cost itself.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The runners who did not finish the full marathon form what percentage of all the runners who did not finish, across the four categories?

solution.concept: Non-finishers = registrations × (100 − finished)%
solution.explanation: Non-finishers: 5 km 120, 10 km 180, half 180, full 180, total 660. The full marathon's share = 180 ÷ 660 = 27.27%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 30% is the full marathon's own non-finishing rate; 25% assumes the four categories share equally; 33.33% leaves out the 5 km race.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the rejection rate of unit U1?

solution.concept: Rejection rate = rejected ÷ stitched × 100
solution.explanation: U1 rejected 96 of the 2,400 shirts it stitched: 96 ÷ 2,400 = 4%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.17% divides by the accepted shirts (2,304); 2.5% inverts part of the calculation; 3.5% is U3's rate.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many shirts did unit U4 stitch?

solution.concept: Accepted shirts are (100 − rejection rate)% of the shirts stitched
solution.explanation: U4 rejected 6%, so the 2,820 accepted shirts are 94% of those stitched: 2,820 ÷ 0.94 = 3,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2,989.2 adds 6% to 2,820 (a percentage of the wrong base); 2,650.8 takes 6% off 2,820; 94% of 3,120 is 2,932.8, not 2,820.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By how many shirts did U3's accepted shirts exceed U2's accepted shirts?

solution.concept: Fill both rows first: U2 stitched = rejected ÷ rate; U3 rejected = stitched × rate
solution.explanation: U2: 150 is 5% of the shirts stitched, so U2 stitched 3,000 and accepted 2,850. U3: 3.5% of 3,200 = 112 rejected, so 3,088 accepted. Difference = 3,088 − 2,850 = 238.
solution.why_others_wrong: 200 compares stitched shirts; 162 subtracts the difference in rejections (38) instead of adding it; 312 has no basis.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the overall rejection rate of the four units taken together (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Overall rate = total rejected ÷ total stitched — not the average of the four rates
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.63% is the simple average of the four rates (4.625%) rounded, which ignores the different volumes; 4.86% divides by the accepted total (11,062); 4.16% leaves out U4 (358 ÷ 8,600).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
