Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: 35% of 260
Quantity II: 28% of 320

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Compute each percentage exactly
solution.explanation: Quantity I = 0.35 × 260 = 91. Quantity II = 0.28 × 320 = 89.6. So Quantity I > Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I < Quantity II' comes from assuming the larger base (320) gives the larger value.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Quantity I > Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: The average of 13, 17, 21, 25 and 29
Quantity II: The median of 12, 30, 19, 24 and 22

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: The average of an evenly spaced list is its middle term; the median is the middle value after sorting
solution.explanation: Quantity I: the numbers rise by 4, so the average is the middle term, 21. Quantity II: sorted, the numbers are 12, 19, 22, 24, 30, so the median is 22. Quantity I < Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I > Quantity II' takes the middle value of II without sorting (19).
solution.final_answer: Option C: Quantity I < Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: Time (in hours) taken by a car at 54 km/h to cover 189 km
Quantity II: Time (in hours) taken by a car at 60 km/h to cover 200 km

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Time = distance ÷ speed
solution.explanation: Quantity I = 189 ÷ 54 = 3.5 hours. Quantity II = 200 ÷ 60 = 3⅓ hours ≈ 3.33 hours. So Quantity I > Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I < Quantity II' assumes the longer distance always takes longer.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Quantity I > Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: The sum of two positive whole numbers whose product is 36
Quantity II: 13

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: List every possible pair before comparing
solution.explanation: Pairs with product 36: (1, 36), (2, 18), (3, 12), (4, 9), (6, 6), with sums 37, 20, 15, 13 and 12. Quantity I can be more than, equal to or less than 13, so the relationship cannot be established.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I ≥ Quantity II' misses the pair (6, 6) with sum 12; 'Quantity I ≤ Quantity II' looks only at (6, 6) and (4, 9).
solution.final_answer: Option A: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: Area (cm²) of an equilateral triangle of side 12 cm (take √3 = 1.73)
Quantity II: Area (cm²) of a circle of diameter 9 cm (take π = 22/7)

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Area of an equilateral triangle = (√3/4)a²; area of a circle = πr² with r = diameter ÷ 2
solution.explanation: Quantity I = 1.73 × 144 ÷ 4 = 1.73 × 36 = 62.28 cm². Quantity II = 22/7 × 4.5² = 22/7 × 20.25 ≈ 63.64 cm². So Quantity I < Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I > Quantity II' comes from using π = 3 instead of the stated 22/7 (3 × 20.25 = 60.75).
solution.final_answer: Option D: Quantity I < Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: Speed (km/h) of a 200 m long train that crosses a 250 m long platform in 30 seconds
Quantity II: 52

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Crossing a platform: distance = train + platform
solution.explanation: Quantity I = (200 + 250) ÷ 30 = 15 m/s = 15 × 18/5 = 54 km/h. So Quantity I > Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I < Quantity II' uses only the train's length (200 ÷ 30 = 6⅔ m/s = 24 km/h).
solution.final_answer: Option A: Quantity I > Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: The number of integers x for which x² < 20
Quantity II: The number of positive divisors of 48

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Count negative integers and zero too; count divisors from the prime factorisation
solution.explanation: Quantity I: x² < 20 holds for x = −4, −3, …, 3, 4, which is 9 integers. Quantity II: 48 = 2⁴ × 3, so it has (4 + 1)(1 + 1) = 10 divisors. So Quantity I < Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: '≥' and '>' come from miscounting the divisors of 48 (for example missing 16 and 24 and getting 8).
solution.final_answer: Option D: Quantity I < Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: The value of x, where 2^(x + 1) + 2^(x − 1) = 80
Quantity II: The value of y, where y² − 11y + 30 = 0

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factor out the smaller power: 2^(x − 1)(2² + 1); a quadratic has two roots to compare against
solution.explanation: Quantity I: 2^(x − 1) × (4 + 1) = 80, so 2^(x − 1) = 16 = 2⁴ and x = 5. Quantity II: (y − 5)(y − 6) = 0, so y = 5 or 6. x equals y in one case and is smaller in the other, so Quantity I ≤ Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I < Quantity II' misses y = 5; 'Quantity I ≥ Quantity II' compares only with y = 5.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Quantity I ≤ Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Each question below is followed by two statements. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.
Question: What is the perimeter of the square?
I. The diagonal of the square is 8√2 cm.
II. The area of the square equals the area of a rectangle measuring 16 cm by 4 cm.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not
Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient
Both statements I and II together are needed

solution.concept: One measurement fixes a square completely
solution.explanation: I: side = diagonal ÷ √2 = 8 cm, so the perimeter is 32 cm — sufficient. II: area = 64 cm², so the side is 8 cm (a length is positive) and the perimeter is 32 cm — sufficient. Either statement alone answers the question.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Both together' is chosen when a candidate does not notice that a square has only one free measurement.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Each question below is followed by two statements. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.
Question: What is the average age of the 30 students of a class (15 boys and 15 girls)?
I. When the class teacher, who is 30 years old, is included, the average age rises by 6 months.
II. The average age of the 15 boys is 15 years.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient
Both statements I and II together are needed
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not

solution.concept: Inclusion changes the total by the new member's age; a group's average needs both sub-group averages
solution.explanation: I: if the class average is a, then 30a + 30 = 31(a + 0.5), so a = 14.5 years — sufficient. II gives the boys' average only; the girls' average is unknown — not sufficient.
steps: II: girls' average unknown ⇒ not sufficient
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Either' assumes the girls' average equals the boys'; 'Both' is not needed because I alone fixes the average.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by three statements. Decide which statements are sufficient to answer it.
Question: What is Neha's monthly income?
I. She saves 20% of her income and spends the rest.
II. Her rent is 30% of her total monthly expenditure.
III. Her monthly rent is ₹9,600.

options.text: Any two of the three statements together are sufficient
All three statements together are necessary
Only statements II and III together are sufficient
Even all three statements together are not sufficient

solution.concept: Chain of percentages: rent = 30% of expenditure = 30% of 80% of income
solution.explanation: With all three: rent = 0.3 × 0.8 × income = 0.24 × income = 9,600, so the income is ₹40,000. Without I, the share of income spent is unknown; without II, the rent's share of spending is unknown; without III, there is no rupee figure. So all three are needed.
steps: I + II: only percentages, no amount
I + III: rent's share of spending unknown
II + III: expenditure = 32,000, but its share of income unknown
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Only II and III' gives the expenditure (₹32,000) but not the income; 'any two' fails for the same reason.
solution.final_answer: Option B: All three statements together are necessary

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Each question below is followed by two statements. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.
Question: What is the rate of interest per annum?
I. A sum lent at this rate of simple interest doubles itself in 8 years.
II. The compound interest for 2 years, compounded annually, on a certain sum at this rate is ₹2,656.25.

options.text: Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient
Both statements I and II together are needed
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not
Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not

solution.concept: A rate can be found from a doubling time, but not from an interest amount on an unknown sum
solution.explanation: I: doubling means the interest equals the principal: R × 8 = 100, so R = 12.5% — sufficient. II: one equation with two unknowns (sum and rate): ₹10,000 at 12.5% fits, but so does a larger sum at a lower rate (about ₹12,649 at 10%) — not sufficient.
steps: I: SI = P in 8 years ⇒ 8R = 100 ⇒ R = 12.5%
II: P[(1 + R/100)² − 1] = 2,656.25 has many (P, R) solutions
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Either' assumes the sum in II is known; 'Both' is unnecessary because I alone fixes the rate.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by three statements. Decide which statements are sufficient to answer it.
Question: What was the population of the town in 2026?
I. The population grew by 10% from 2024 to 2025 and by 12% from 2025 to 2026.
II. The population in 2024 was 50,000.
III. The population increased by 6,600 from 2025 to 2026.

options.text: Only I and II together are sufficient
Any two of the three statements together are sufficient
All three statements together are necessary
Either I and II together or I and III together are sufficient

solution.concept: Check every pair; a pair works only if it fixes one base value and the growth that follows it
solution.explanation: I + II: 50,000 × 1.1 × 1.12 = 61,600 — sufficient. I + III: 12% of the 2025 population = 6,600, so the 2025 population was 55,000 and 2026's was 61,600 — sufficient. II + III: the growth from 2024 to 2025 is unknown, so the 2025 base for the 6,600 is unknown (for example 10% then 12%, or 20% then 11%, give 61,600 or 66,600) — not sufficient. No statement alone is enough.
steps: II + III: two unknown growth rates ⇒ not sufficient
Answer: I with II, or I with III
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Only I and II' misses that III can replace II; 'any two' wrongly includes II + III.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Either I and II together or I and III together are sufficient
